units.label: 跨叙事、提示的离散事件分割比较
units.description: 三篇故事及Pieman两次既有人类运行共享方法；原始/long提示和六次模型重复是条件/重复，不计独立行为实验。

units.label: 模型复制、滑窗及边界概率时间对齐
units.description: text-davinci-002生成、GPT2 tokenization、forced alignment及DTW服务离散和连续比较；并非本文训练模型。

units.label: 既有人类共识与个体/连续概率比较
units.description: 复用三项历史人类数据；个体对共识和概率时序分析使用共享分割结果，Monkey随机拼接四段形成30个合成人类向量。

facts.statement: 研究连续自然叙事的GPT-3事件边界能否接近人类共识，并区分共识标注用途与个体认知测量；细粒度和long提示是本文比较。

method_function.text: 界定事件分割效标及提示条件

facts.statement: 材料为三篇故事：Pieman约7分30秒、Monkey约30分钟、Tunnel约25分钟。Pieman两次人类运行来自同一205人；Monkey四季度不同批人，Tunnel10人；不是四/五个独立新实验。

method_function.text: 识别故事、运行、参与者层次

facts.statement: UTF-8故事转录无连字符，去引号和省略号；pretrained GPT2 fast tokenizer分词，Penn Phonetics Lab Forced Aligner把词与音频毫秒位置对齐。

method_function.text: 文本清洗与音文对齐

facts.statement: 实际调用text-davinci-002 completion，要求逐字复制并以换行划事件，故事前后均有指令；long条件除首个定义之外在event前加long，以获得粗粒度分割。

method_function.text: 操纵事件粒度

facts.statement: 温度0；4096上下文只用2048，先扣指令token，再把余量平分输入故事与max_tokens输出；Tunnel因截断额外加512输出token。

method_function.text: 控制复制偏离与输出截断

facts.statement: 滑窗输出按换行拆事件，下窗从上窗最后一个模型边界开始，把末尾未完成事件重新置于下一输入；直到故事完成，最终边界列表可串接，作者称不产生重叠边界。

method_function.text: 长故事分块与尾段续接

facts.statement: 温度0仍非完全确定，首次分割后各故事各提示再重复五次，共六次；不同重复确会产生不同解，并用模型解间最大Hamming距离描述差异。

method_function.text: 经验重复稳定性核查

facts.statement: 人类Pieman205人听并划分两次；Monkey所有人听完整故事但各只标自己季度，样本30/35/31/42；Tunnel10人线下。前两研究用MTurk，本文复用先前已发表标注。

method_function.text: 既有比较样本与分段分母

facts.statement: 人类按空格标自然有意义单元转换。共识先把个体响应转为毫秒0/1向量，Pieman按±500ms、其他按±1s扩展，再平均。

method_function.text: 从按键形成群体响应概率

facts.statement: 共识平均曲线用Gaussian平滑：Pieman宽2s、95百分位阈值；Monkey/Tunnel σ=.2s、find_peaks且90百分位，邻近簇取最大峰；后两故事同一子句后的重复边界人工删较小者。此检测在原研究已完成。

method_function.text: 共识边界构造与人工去重

facts.statement: 方法段把个体按键和聚合边界归到最近句边界，时间为前句末词offset与后句首词onset平均；平均位移Pieman1.068/.792s、Monkey1.64s、Tunnel3.368s，Tunnel最大27.981s。讨论另写next句边界，未消除二者差别。

method_function.text: 句级离散化用于模型人类比较

facts.statement: 每个句边界编码是否事件0/1，以不一致位数/全部句边界数得归一Hamming距离，误放与遗漏均增距；如[1,0,0]与[1,1,0]为1/3。

method_function.text: 透明句级不一致比例

facts.statement: 将真实Hamming与100000次随机句序置换距离分布比较，p为随机条件距离更小的比例；文中未给加一修正，不擅补。

method_function.text: 句序置换机会基线

facts.statement: 另把1−Hamming相似度相对于给定GPT/人类边界数允许的最小和最大相似度归一，跨六次取平均，作者报告置换p不变。

method_function.text: 控制边界数量约束的相对相似度
离散边界一致性结果

facts.statement: 六次重复有不同边界解且并非每个解均通过机会基线；原始Monkey另解p=.074/.069，long Pieman另解第一次人类运行p=.216。

method_function.text: 重复结果限制

facts.statement: 个体比较计算每个人对群体共识距离，以及每次GPT解对相同共识距离，再作独立样本双侧t检验。Monkey为四季度各随机不放回选人并拼接，构造30份全故事响应向量。

method_function.text: 个体/模型解到同一共识的比较

facts.statement: 原始提示GPT比Pieman人类首次更接近共识(p=.045)，第二次差异不显著(p=.46)，Monkey p=.005；long三个比较均p<.001。Tunnel未纳入这项个体共识比较，正文理由是前两故事有足够标注。

method_function.text: 个体对共识比较结果及范围

facts.statement: 连续人类概率用未平滑个体响应向量平均比例再取log；模型请求top5 token logprob取newline，跨六次平均。newline不在top5则未定义而非0，平均57.375%token有该值。

method_function.text: 连续边界强度读出

facts.statement: 词时间均分到GPT2子token；用GPT2LMHeadModel词嵌入及fastdtw Euclidean路径将生成tokens映射至转录tokens和时间。毫秒NaN向量在有newline top5的token整个onset–offset区间填logprob，其余NaN一维线性插值。

method_function.text: 生成文本到音频时间轴映射

facts.statement: 人类零响应时log未定义并插值，随后两时序作cross-correlation，检验零lag与0差异；为人类感知动作延迟还搜索lag作为相关上界，图3纵轴明确Pearson r。

method_function.text: 连续时间关联与时滞比较

facts.statement: 原始提示零lag r Pieman .308/.362，Monkey .092；long .311/.369/.102，均报告p<.001。最大相关位于非零正lag；Monkey较低相关可能因小样本噪声是作者解释。

method_function.text: 连续边界概率关联结果

facts.statement: 作者指出人类听音频而GPT只看文本；GPT可利用当前及下一事件的完整片段，初次人类在线按键仅有过去信息，Pieman第二次可能利用记忆；句级化丢弃句内信号，英语西方样本限制外推。

method_function.text: 限定模态、前瞻信息、粒度和群体适用范围

facts.statement: long边界不总是细边界的子集；更复杂定义易偏离逐字复制、去定义趋向日常occurrence为作者所述提示观察，外部补充材料另载轶事，不当作本文正式独立条件的完整数据。

method_function.text: 提示敏感性和未读外部补充边界

facts.statement: 本文是既有GPT3零样本应用及历史人类数据再分析；GPT预训练描述是背景，不是本文自行训练。作者开放数据代码于Zenodo并报告原研究IRB及知情同意；尚未运行代码复现。

method_function.text: 训练来源与可得性界定

Prompting In order to prompt GPT-3 to segment a continuous story into events, a completion was created with the
model version “text-davinci-002” (beta.openai.com/docs/
models/). In completion, the model is asked to complete the
provided prompt by predicting upcoming tokens. The specific prompt for the model was: “An event is an ongoing
coherent situation. The following story needs to be copied
and segmented into events. Copy the following story wordfor-word and start a new line whenever one event ends and
another begins. This is the story:”. After this instruction,
a segment from the story was inserted (we split the full
story into shorter segments, see next paragraph). Finally,
after a new line, an additional prompt segment was added
to refresh the instruction: “This is a word-for-word copy of
the same story that is segmented into events:”. In a variation of the instruction, the qualifier “long” was added before
every occurrence of the word event in the prompt, with the
exception of the first definition. This was done to obtain a
coarse-grained event segmentation.

Results
Event segmentations from GPT-3 significantly align
with consensus human annotations

in the Middle” and “Tunnel Under the World” into discrete
events using GPT-3 (version “text-davinci-002”). “Pieman”
was segmented into 23 events by GPT-3 (compared to 19

Preprocessing Transcriptions of these auditory stories were
used for their segmentation with GPT-3 in this study. Transcriptions were in plain text (UTF-8 encoding), no hyphens
were present, and quotation marks and occurrences of
ellipses were removed. Subsequently, the words were transformed into tokens; tokens are the units of text in large
language models, for instance, one way of tokenizing the
word “tokenizer ” could be into “token” and “izer”. The
fast implementation of the pretrained GPT-2 tokenizer was
used to tokenize the text (huggingface.co). The transcripts
were aligned to the audio recordings via Penn Phonetics Lab
Forced Aligner (Yuan & Liberman, 2008). This was done
to later match behavioral button press responses (that had
been recorded in milliseconds from the start of the audio) to
positions in the text.

Properties and hyperparameters The input that GPT-3 can
process is limited to 4096 tokens. Only text within this socalled context window can affect predictions of the model.
Additionally, a temperature parameter controls the degree
to which randomness affects the model output. A lower temperature makes the output more deterministic, while a higher
temperature makes it more creative. To increase reproducibility, the temperature parameter was set to 0. Additionally, only
half of the width of the context window (i.e., 4096/2 = 2048)
was used, because the model output occasionally diverged

Sliding window for long stories The context length of the
GPT-3 model that we used was not long enough to encompass
each of the three stories. Therefore, we used a sliding window approach to split the stories into segments that fit into the
context length of GPT-3. The length of a story segment was
determined based on the number of input and output tokens
that fit into the context window (see below for some notes on
the width that was used for the context window). The output
text that the model generated was then split into events at
newline characters. After processing the first story segment
this way, we defined the next segment by starting at the final
model-identified event boundary in the first segment, and
then continuing forward with as much of the story as would
fit given constraints on context window size. We continued
with this process until the entire story had been fed into the
model. Note that, in this scheme, any “trailing” tokens falling
between the final model-identified event boundary of a segment and actual end of that segment were simply reassigned
to be the start of the next segment. I.e., when the final event
in a story segment stopped before the end of the full story, the
next story segment was taken from the beginning of the final

Continuous segmentation probability Another way to analyze behavioral responses is to compute the probability of
button presses at every moment in the story. Similarly, predictions in GPT-3 can be treated as probabilistic. In order
to compare the probability of event boundaries directly, we,
therefore, log-transformed human event annotations to obtain
the log-probability of a button press throughout the story.
For GPT-3, we derived a continuous output variable from
the log-probability of the newline character for every token
in the story (averaged across 6 iterations of the model) with
the following procedure: The log-probability of the top 5
predicted tokens was requested in the completion (which
was the maximum number of token-probabilities that could
be requested by the user at the time of preparation of this
manuscript). The log-probability of the newline character
was then used to assess to what degree the model predicted
an event boundary at any given token in the story. Whenever
the newline character was not among the top 5 predicted
tokens, the log-probability was not defined. Note that, on
average, 57.375 % of tokens entailed the newline character among the top 5 predictions (min = 52.833 %, max =
61.438 %). To interpolate the token-probabilities onto the
same time axis as the behavioral data, the onset and offset
times of words in the transcript were used. Words from the
transcript were converted to tokens with the pretrained GPT2 tokenizer; whenever a word was converted to more than one
token, the interval spanned by its onset and offset was evenly

split among the resulting tokens which yielded token-onset
and -offset times. Next, all words from a given GPT-3 generated response were tokenized and word embeddings from
the GPT-2 Model transformer (GPT2LMHeadModel) were
used to map model-output tokens onto the list of aligned
tokens from the transcript via dynamic-time-warping (using
the fastdtw implementation Salvador and Chan, 2007, distance metric: Euclidean distance). The warp path was then
applied to the token-onset and -offset times, which resulted
in an onset and offset for every token that was generated by
GPT-3. Finally, a vector of NaN values of the same length
as the time-axis of the story was generated; for those tokens
where a newline character was among the top-5 predicted
tokens, the value of that vector was set to the log-probability
of the newline character in the whole interval between the
token’s onset and offset time. The outcome of this transformation was a vector of the same length as the behavioral
response vector from the human participants; the vector held
the log-probability of the newline character whenever it was
among the top-5 predicted tokens and NaN otherwise. NaN
values were then interpolated with one-dimensional linear
interpolation.

Human event segmentation
To assess the quality of GPT-3’s automated event segmentation, we compared the event boundaries segmented by GPT-3
to those annotated by large numbers of human participants.
Data from the human behavioral event segmentation tasks
were previously analyzed and published, and were made
available by the authors upon our request. In this subsection,
we describe the details of these datasets, which are summarized in Table 1.
Experimental paradigm Participants in the first two studies
were recruited via Amazon’s Mechanical Turk (Buhrmester
et al., 2011). Event segmentations for the “Pieman” story
were obtained from 205 participants that listened to the story

twice and also segmented the story twice (Michelmann et
al., 2021), i.e., data from two behavioral runs were available.
The verbatim instruction for these participants was: “press
the space bar every time when, in your judgment, one natural and meaningful unit ends and another begins”. Event
segmentation for “Monkey in the Middle” was obtained with
the same instructions, however, batches of participants annotated 4 sections of the story that were similar in length: All
participants listened to the full story but only segmented their
respective section; a total of 30 participants segmented the
first quarter, 35 participants segmented the second quarter,
31 participants segmented the third quarter, and 42 participants segmented the final quarter of the story (Kumar et al.,
2022). Event segmentation for “Tunnel Under the World”
was obtained from 10 participants that participated in person
(Lositsky et al., 2016).

GPT-3 segmentation is no longer significantly better. For
“Monkey in the Middle”, we treated concatenated response
vectors from the four different segments (selected at random without replacement) as a single participant. These 30
combined data sets had an average Hamming distance of
0.302 (S D = 0.094) to the consensus solution (derived
from the average across all participants). Again, the GPT3-derived solutions were significantly more similar to the
consensus solution with an average Hamming distance of
0.249 (S D = 0.001, p = 0.005) supporting the idea that
GPT-3-derived segmentations are closer to a consensus solution that large samples of human raters converge on (see
Fig. 2).
We next repeated this analysis with the long event segmentation prompt. For “Pieman” the average Hamming distance
of long GPT-3-derived segmentations to the consensus solution was 0.23 (S D = 0.01) for the first behavioral run and
0.199, (S D = 0.01) for the second behavioral run. Both of
these values were significantly lower than the average for
human annotations ( p < 0.001 in both cases). For “Monkey
in the Middle”, the average Hamming distance of long GPT3-derived segmentations to the consensus solution was 0.187
(S D = 0.003), which was significantly lower than the average for human annotations ( p < 0.001). The lower Hamming
distances under the long event segmentation prompt suggest
that these long events may be closer to shared human perception.

Comparison of boundary probabilities between
GPT-3 and human annotators
The event boundaries from human participants are those
moments where a substantial amount of people pressed a
button within a certain time window (i.e., peaks in agreement). That is, human event boundaries are discrete measures
derived from a continuous variable (ratio of responses).
Another way to treat this measure, however, is as the probability of button presses at every moment in the story. Similarly,
predictions in GPT-3 can be treated as probabilistic. In order
to compare the probability of event boundaries directly, we,
therefore, log-transformed human event annotations to obtain
the log-probability of a button press throughout the story. For
GPT-3, we derived a continuous output variable from the logprobability of the newline character for every token in the
story (averaged across all 6 iterations of the model) and we
interpolated those values onto the same time axis (in milliseconds, based on the audio; see Section “Methods” for detail).
We then computed the cross-correlation between those time
courses (note that we did not expect a specific lag between
the time-courses, however, because human responses may
entail a perception-to-action delay, we computed the crosscorrelation to obtain an upper bound of the true correlation,

Discussion
Here we demonstrate that GPT-3 can segment a continuous narrative into events, akin to the way human annotators
perform this task. A key benefit of our approach is that it
is more scalable to very long naturalistic stimuli as obtaining human-derived annotations for very long stimuli can be
prohibitively labor- and resource-intensive. GPT-3 derived
boundaries were also significantly closer to the “consensus”
solution, on average, than boundaries identified by individual human annotators. These findings suggest that GPT-3 is
a feasible method for cognitive scientists that are interested
in event segmentation. When individual human annotations
are expected to be noisy and large behavioral samples are not
available, a language model that has been trained on 45TB
of text may be a useful alternative to obtain normative information about human text perception.

instead of relying on a few curated examples. Importantly, the
variance between human annotators may contain meaningful information about individual human event perception; it
is therefore important to note that, despite GPT-3’s ability to
capture human event perception, human behavioral data cannot be replaced as the gold standard for the investigation of
human cognition. That is, studies that investigate individual
segmentation behavior and are not interested in a consensus solution should refrain from using boundary annotations
derived from Large Language Models. In a similar vein, systematic differences between human event annotations and
annotations from large language models may become the
subject of investigation.

Methods
We develop a simple approach to enable GPT-3 to segment
narrative stories into meaningful events, utilizing zero-shot
prompting. We validate this approach across three stories
of different lengths, and compare the resulting GPT-3 event
segmentations with annotations from human participants.

Materials
Stimuli We tested our approach on narrative stories of three
different lengths, which were previously used in psychological and neuroscientific experiments: 1) “Pieman”, a short
story of 7 min and 30 s that was presented at a live storytelling
event at the Moth (O’Grady, 2008). “Pieman” is a humorous autobiographic description of the narrator’s struggle with
journalistic integrity when he started his career in journalism
at the student newspaper of his university. 2) “Monkey in

the Middle”, a 30-min-long audio podcast that appeared on
“This American Life” (Chavis, 2017). It describes the events
surrounding a famous legal case about copyright infringement; in this case PETA argued that the copyright to the
photographs that monkeys took of themselves belongs to the
monkeys. 3) “The Tunnel Under the World”, a 25-min-long
science fiction story that was broadcast on the radio show “X
Minus One” (Pohl, 1956). The story follows Guy Burckhardt,
who wakes up on June 15th with a vivid nightmare. As he
goes about his day, he notices strange occurrences. The next
day, he wakes up again on June 15th, realizing he is reliving
the same day over and over.

used for their segmentation with GPT-3 in this study. Transcriptions were in plain text (UTF-8 encoding), no hyphens
were present, and quotation marks and occurrences of
ellipses were removed. Subsequently, the words were transformed into tokens; tokens are the units of text in large
language models, for instance, one way of tokenizing the
word “tokenizer ” could be into “token” and “izer”. The
fast implementation of the pretrained GPT-2 tokenizer was
used to tokenize the text (huggingface.co). The transcripts
were aligned to the audio recordings via Penn Phonetics Lab
Forced Aligner (Yuan & Liberman, 2008). This was done
to later match behavioral button press responses (that had
been recorded in milliseconds from the start of the audio) to
positions in the text.

Properties and hyperparameters The input that GPT-3 can
process is limited to 4096 tokens. Only text within this socalled context window can affect predictions of the model.
Additionally, a temperature parameter controls the degree
to which randomness affects the model output. A lower temperature makes the output more deterministic, while a higher
temperature makes it more creative. To increase reproducibility, the temperature parameter was set to 0. Additionally, only
half of the width of the context window (i.e., 4096/2 = 2048)
was used, because the model output occasionally diverged

Sliding window for long stories The context length of the
GPT-3 model that we used was not long enough to encompass
each of the three stories. Therefore, we used a sliding window approach to split the stories into segments that fit into the
context length of GPT-3. The length of a story segment was
determined based on the number of input and output tokens
that fit into the context window (see below for some notes on
the width that was used for the context window). The output
text that the model generated was then split into events at
newline characters. After processing the first story segment
this way, we defined the next segment by starting at the final
model-identified event boundary in the first segment, and
then continuing forward with as much of the story as would
fit given constraints on context window size. We continued
with this process until the entire story had been fed into the
model. Note that, in this scheme, any “trailing” tokens falling
between the final model-identified event boundary of a segment and actual end of that segment were simply reassigned
to be the start of the next segment. I.e., when the final event
in a story segment stopped before the end of the full story, the
next story segment was taken from the beginning of the final

event of the previous segment and continued into the story for
the next completion request. The segmentation was complete
after all text from a given story had been parsed. Note that
our sliding window does not produce overlap in event segmentation, because all information in the final event (where
no further event boundaries are detected) becomes the beginning of the next segment, i.e., there is no overlapping event
boundary and the event boundaries in the subsequent segment can simply be concatenated to the event boundaries in
the previous segment.

Human consensus estimation, event annotation, and sentence boundary alignment Aggregated event boundaries
were derived for all data by computing smoothed averages
across participants and detecting local peaks in the time
course of the agreement. Specifically, for the “Pieman” story,
individual participants’ data were aggregated in response
vectors at a millisecond resolution that were set to 1 if a
response was recorded within the surrounding second (i.e.,
within 500 ms in either direction) and to 0 otherwise. For the
stories “Monkey in the Middle” and “The Tunnel Under the
World”, data were aggregated in response vectors in the same
way; however, because less data were available, a response
was marked within the 2-s interval around button presses
(i.e., within 1 s in either direction).

The averaged response vector was then smoothed with
a Gaussian kernel and thresholded. For the “Pieman” story
time-courses were smoothed with a Gaussian kernel of 2-s
width; time-courses of “Monkey in the Middle” and “The
Tunnel Under the World” were smoothed with a kernel
with a standard deviation of 0.2 s, which corresponds to
an interval of approximately 1 s in the smoothing kernel.
Finally, the smoothed agreement was thresholded at the 95th
percentile for the “Pieman” story. For the stories “Monkey in the Middle” and “The Tunnel Under the World”,
boundary points were computed using the Python function scipy.signal.find_peaks and thresholded at
the 90th percentile.

To compare the distances between event annotations at the
sentence level, a vector was created that held zero for each
sentence boundary that was not an event boundary, and one

for each sentence boundary that was also an event boundary.
Two event annotations were then compared by computing the

Comparison to other normed measures of similarity
Previous work on event segmentation in humans has reported
normalized measures of correlation between raters. Specifically, Kurby and Zacks (2011) report a normalized pointbiserial correlation, where correlations are expressed relative
to the minimum and maximum correlation possible given the
number of boundaries a participant identified. We adopted
this approach for comparison purposes and expressed similarity values (1-Hamming distance) relative to the maximum
and minimum similarity, given the number of boundaries that
GPT-3 and human annotators identified. Without the long
qualifier, we obtained relative similarity values of 0.444 and
0.482 for the first and second behavioral run of the “Pieman”
story, averaging across all replications. For “Monkey in the
Middle”, the average relative similarity was 0.321 and for
“Tunnel Under the World” we obtained a relative similarity
of 0.655. When including the long qualifier, we obtained an
average relative similarity of 0.359 and 0.513 with the first
and second behavioral run of the “Pieman” story. We further observed a relative similarity of 0.262 for “Monkey in
the Middle”, and 0.379 for “Tunnel Under the World”. Note
that all p values remained identical because the permutation
statistic is scale invariant.

Notably, the present results may represent a lower bound
of the similarity between GPT-3-derived annotations and
human event perception, because human participants in our
study segmented the audio form of the narrative, whereas
GPT-3 only had access to the text itself. In the audio form
of the narrative, the speaker may convey information about
event structure via pauses and intonation that are absent from
the text and they may obscure events by rapidly connecting consecutive sentences. Furthermore, GPT-3 performed
event segmentation based on a full text-segment; therein, the
model could use information from the current and next event
to place an event boundary. In contrast, human annotators

had to make button-press decisions only based on past information (with the notable exemption of the second behavioral
run of the “Pieman” story, where human participants could
use their memory of the text to improve their segmentation). Conversely, GPT-derived boundaries could only be
resolved at a sentence-level resolution. The attribution of
human event boundaries to the next sentence boundary effectively treats the occurrence of mid-sentence boundaries as
“noise” to be removed by the analysis, whereas some of
these responses may be cognitive “signal” that is of interest
to the experimenter. This is an important limitation of this
approach. Future research may investigate the importance
of such differences between GPT-3 and human perception
further. Additionally, our evaluation uses datasets that are
representative of those commonly studied in human cognitive science and has, for instance, been successfully applied
in recent work to analyze a new text domain and dataset:
free-form autobiographical memories from over 1000 participants (Rouhani et al., 2023). It is, however, important to
note that those datasets are not representative of the entire
world population (e.g., they are in English and are Westernfocused). Researchers who want to build on our methods
should consider the similarity of their experimental stimulus
and participant population.

In this study, we tested prompt variations that changed the
segmentation behavior of GPT-3 from a fine-grained segmentation to a coarser segmentation. This coarse segmentation
appeared to match human behavior better. However, future
work may explore if responses from human subjects that are
instructed to segment the smallest units that seem natural to
them (Zacks et al., 2007) align more closely with the GPTderived segmentation without the long qualifier. It is also
noteworthy that the long GPT-derived event boundaries are
not always a subset of the small event boundaries, which can
happen in GPT and humans, for instance, when a coherent
train of thought spans two separate larger events (e.g., two
time periods).
We also cannot rule out that – with further prompt engineering – a different prompt will provide an even more
human-like segmentation than the prompt that we used. In the
Supplementary material, we discuss some anecdotal observations on prompt variations. Notably, expanding the definition
of event often resulted in text output that diverged from a
word-for-word copy; removing the definition of “event”, on
the other hand, resulted in a segmentation that appeared to
be based on the colloquial understanding of event as “occurrence” (e.g., a person stopping).

The current approach examines whether a powerful large
language model, GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020), can segment
events in a similar way to humans. Specifically, we assess its
ability to perform event segmentation tasks using only zeroshot prompting (i.e., without any additional fine-tuning or
in-context learning). We prompt GPT-3 with a similar (albeit
simpler) prompt to what human participants are shown when
asked to segment a naturalistic stimulus into meaningful
events. Across a variety of stories, we find that GPT-3 is able
to perform this task significantly above chance. Moreover,
we demonstrate that GPT-derived event boundaries provide
a good approximation of the consensus solution (obtained
by averaging responses across people); the boundaries identified by GPT-3 are closer to the consensus, on average, than
boundaries identified by individual human annotators. This
suggests that GPT-3 segments event boundaries according
to a shared human perception that is captured by averaging across large samples of human annotators. Finally, we
derive a continuous measure of event probability from the
log-probability of the newline character (that was used to
indicate a new event) in the model output. This continuous
measure of event boundary perception in the model significantly correlates with the continuous measure of agreement
between human raters. This finding provides further evidence
that GPT-3 can represent the event structure of a natural
story in its predictions, rendering it a feasible tool for obtaining automated event annotations. We will make our code
available to enable others to easily integrate the proposed
approach into their analyses.

GPT-3 event segmentation
Generative Pre-trained Transformer 3 (GPT-3) is a large
language model developed by OpenAI. It can generate
human-like text based on the input it receives (Brown et
al., 2020). GPT-3 is built on the transformer architecture
(Vaswani et al., 2023), which uses self-attention mechanisms
to process input text; it effectively weighs the importance of
different words in a sentence to generate output. To learn how
to generate its output, GPT-3 is trained on a vast corpus of
text data from the Internet to predict the next word in a sentence. Therein, the model’s weights are adjusted according
to the error in its prediction.
